root.label: Weimar & Nazi Germany
root.gloss: Germany from First World War defeat and Weimar democracy in 1918 through Hitler's rise to a totalitarian Nazi dictatorship by August 1939.

children.label: KT1: The Weimar Republic
children.gloss: Key topic 1: The Weimar Republic, 1918–29 — origins amid war collapse, early 1919–23 crises, Stresemann's recovery, and Weimar social and cultural change.

children.label: 1.1 Origins of the Republic
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues the Republic was crippled from birth by armistice shame and Article 48 flaws vs View 2 argues Ebert and progressive democratic rights saved Germany from chaos.

children.label: Unrest, Abdication & Armistice
children.gloss: Situation in Germany at the end of the War brought political unrest, the abdication of the Kaiser, the November armistice, and a new republic.

children.label: Allied Blockade & Kiel Mutiny
children.gloss: Blockade shortages killed 750,000 civilians; 40,000 Kiel sailors mutinied (Nov 1918).

children.label: Wilhelm II Fled to Holland
children.gloss: Kaiser lost army loyalty at Spa; Scheidemann proclaimed Republic (9 Nov).

children.label: Kaiser lost army loyalty at Spa
children.gloss: Kaiser lost army loyalty at Spa

children.label: Armistice → 'Stab in the Back' Myth
children.gloss: Erzberger signed 11 November armistice; Nationalists branded democrats traitors.

children.label: Ebert-Groener Pact Averted Chaos
children.gloss: Secured Imperial Army & civil service; Prevented Bolshevik-style civil war.

children.label: Weimar Constitution Design
children.gloss: The new Weimar Constitution combined progressive democratic strengths in Germany with dangerous structural weaknesses.

children.label: National Assembly Met in Weimar
children.gloss: Violent street fighting shook Berlin; Deputies met in Weimar (Feb 1919).

children.label: 83% Turnout Backed Moderate Rule
children.gloss: SPD, Centre, DDP won 75%+ seats; Strong democratic mandate in Jan 1919.

children.label: PR & Article 48 → Weak Coalitions
children.gloss: PR splintered Reichstag into 29 parties; Article 48 decrees bypassed Parliament.

children.label: Universal Vote at Age Twenty
children.gloss: Equal male and female suffrage; Free speech & elected 7-year President.

children.label: 1.2 Early Weimar Challenges
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues the Treaty of Versailles and 1923 Ruhr hyperinflation dealt the Republic its worst blow vs View 2 argues armed Left and Right revolts posed the deadlier danger.

children.label: Versailles & Stab in the Back
children.gloss: Early unpopularity of the Republic stemmed from the stab in the back theory and harsh key terms of the Treaty of Versailles.

children.label: Allied Diktat Forced Signature
children.gloss: Allies threatened renewed invasion; Ministers signed treaty (28 June 1919).

children.label: Article 231 & £6.6bn Reparations
children.gloss: War guilt & 100,000-man army cap; No planes/U-boats; lost 13% of land.

children.label: Dolchstoss → Fuelled Right Putsches
children.gloss: Hindenburg claimed army was betrayed; Permanently alienated nationalist voters.

children.label: Peace Preserved National Unity
children.gloss: Prevented foreign breakup of Germany; Bought young democracy breathing space.

children.label: Spartacists, Freikorps & Kapp
children.gloss: Violent challenges to the Republic from Left and Right included the Spartacists, the Freikorps, and the 1920 Kapp Putsch.

children.label: Extremists Rejected Democracy
children.gloss: Spartacists wanted Soviet-style councils; Ex-soldiers hated Versailles army cuts.

children.label: 376 Political Murders by 1922
children.gloss: Organisation Consul squads killed rivals; Assassinated Erzberger & Walther Rathenau.

children.label: Workers Defeated the Kapp Coup
children.gloss: Reichswehr refused to fire on Kapp; Berlin general strike saved Ebert (1920).

children.label: Reichswehr refused to fire on Kapp
children.gloss: Reichswehr refused to fire on Kapp

children.label: Army & Judges Backed the Right
children.gloss: Freikorps killed Luxemburg & Liebknecht; Judges spared right-wing putschists.

children.label: Ruhr Crisis & Hyperinflation
children.gloss: Challenges of 1923 centred on hyperinflation alongside the reasons for and effects of the French occupation of the Ruhr.

children.label: Missed Coal Debt Sparked Invasion
children.gloss: Germany defaulted on coal reparations; 60,000 Franco-Belgian troops seized Ruhr.

children.label: → Triggered 1923 Hyperinflation Crisis
children.gloss: Government printed notes for strikers; Bread reached 200bn marks (Nov 1923).

children.label: Middle-Class Savers Lost Everything
children.gloss: Savings and fixed pensions wiped out; Turned middle classes against Weimar.

children.label: Savings and fixed pensions wiped out
children.gloss: Savings and fixed pensions wiped out

children.label: → Prompted Stresemann's 1923 Recovery
children.gloss: Debtors cleared loans with cheap marks; Stresemann restored currency & order.

children.label: Debtors cleared loans with cheap marks
children.gloss: Debtors cleared loans with cheap marks

children.label: 1.3 Recovery of the Republic
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues Stresemann achieved genuine economic recovery and international acceptance vs View 2 argues Weimar stability stayed a fragile volcano built on short-term US loans.

children.label: Stresemann & the Rentenmark
children.gloss: Economic recovery began when Gustav Stresemann ended passive resistance and stabilized currency with the new Rentenmark.

children.label: Halted Ruhr Strike & Burnt Notes
children.gloss: Ended passive resistance (Sept 1923); Stopped note printing; reopened plants.

children.label: Land-Backed Reichsmark in 1924
children.gloss: Rentenmark tied to land & industry; Restored shopkeeper trust overnight.

children.label: Restored Confidence & Moderate Votes
children.gloss: Sound currency revived domestic trade; Boosted pro-Weimar votes (Dec 1924).

children.label: 1923 Savers Never Fully Repaid
children.gloss: Denied full compensation for lost cash; Ruined pensioners stayed anti-Weimar.

children.label: Denied full compensation for lost cash
children.gloss: Denied full compensation for lost cash

children.label: Dawes, Young & American Loans
children.gloss: The Dawes and Young Plans restructured reparations while American loans and investment funded Weimar economic recovery.

children.label: 800m Gold Marks Kickstarted Output
children.gloss: 1924 Dawes Plan ended Ruhr occupation; Industrial output doubled by 1928.

children.label: Young Plan Cut Bill to £1.85bn
children.gloss: 1929 Young Plan cut debt 75%; Extended annual payments until 1988.

children.label: Exports & Factories Surpassed 1913
children.gloss: $2.5bn Wall Street capital flowed in; Modernised chemical & steel plants.

children.label: Recallable US Loans → 1929 Crash Trap
children.gloss: Stresemann warned of 'volcano' credit; Recallable US loans left Germany exposed.

children.label: Recallable US loans left Germany exposed
children.gloss: Recallable US loans left Germany exposed

children.label: Locarno Pact & League Entry
children.gloss: Stresemann gained international acceptance of Germany through the Locarno Pact and joining the League of Nations.

children.label: Fulfilment Diplomacy Built Trust
children.gloss: Accepted western borders (Locarno 1925); Ended Germany's postwar pariah status.

children.label: Permanent League Council Seat 1926
children.gloss: Joined League Council; signed Kellogg; Secured early Allied Rhineland exit.

children.label: Peaceful Revision Won Allied Respect
children.gloss: Stresemann won 1926 Nobel Peace Prize; Ended French threats of Ruhr invasion.

children.label: Ended French threats of Ruhr invasion
children.gloss: Ended French threats of Ruhr invasion

children.label: Right Attacked Treaty Appeasement
children.gloss: Hugenberg & Hitler condemned Young Plan; Branded Locarno a cowardly betrayal.

children.label: 1.4 Weimar Society & Culture
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues 1924–29 delivered progressive Golden Years in living standards, female equality, and culture vs View 2 argues gains remained uneven and provoked fierce conservative backlash.

children.label: Wages, Homes & Living Standards
children.gloss: Changes in the standard of living brought rising industrial wages, council housing, and welfare insurance.

children.label: Real Wages Rose Over 25 Percent
children.gloss: Union deals lifted skilled urban pay; Highest industrial wages in Europe.

children.label: Union deals lifted skilled urban pay
children.gloss: Union deals lifted skilled urban pay

children.label: 1927 Unemployment Insurance Act
children.gloss: Protected 17 million German workers; Councils built over 2 million homes.

children.label: Housing Shortage Cut by Two-Thirds
children.gloss: Eight-hour shifts & war pensions; Modern flats boosted worker security.

children.label: Farmers & Clerks Faced Slump
children.gloss: Grain gluts bankrupted farms by 1928; White-collar joblessness stayed high.

children.label: Women in Work, Politics & Leisure
children.gloss: Changes in the position of women transformed work, politics, and leisure for urban young Germans.

children.label: Equal Rights & White-Collar Jobs
children.gloss: Article 109 guaranteed civic equality; Offices & stores hired female typists.

children.label: 112 Female Deputies Elected by 1933
children.gloss: 90% female turnout; doctors doubled; Bobbed-hair 'New Women' went out solo.

children.label: Broadest Female Freedom in Europe
children.gloss: Retail & civil service independence; Broke rigid imperial patriarchy.

children.label: 33% Pay Gap & Double Burden
children.gloss: Earned 33% less; zero Cabinet women; Churches attacked falling birth rates.

children.label: Architecture, Art & Weimar Cinema
children.gloss: Cultural changes brought bold developments in Bauhaus architecture, New Objectivity art, and Expressionist cinema.

children.label: Ending Censorship Freed Creators
children.gloss: Constitution protected free expression; Artists challenged war & class greed.

children.label: Gropius, Otto Dix & Fritz Lang
children.gloss: Bauhaus steel-and-glass functionalism; Dix war paintings & Lang's Metropolis.

children.label: Berlin Led Global Modernist Culture
children.gloss: Dietrich films & Brecht's radical stage; Remarque's anti-war novel sold millions.

children.label: Rural Voters Condemned Decadence
children.gloss: Conservatives hated Berlin cabaret clubs; Nazis branded modern art 'degenerate'.

children.label: KT2: Hitler's Rise to Power
children.gloss: Key topic 2: Hitler's rise to power, 1919–33 — founding the NSDAP and SA, the 1923 Munich Putsch and reorganisation, Great Depression surge, and January 1933 appointment.

children.label: 2.1 Early Nazi Party Growth
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues Hitler's spellbinding oratory and Führerprinzip leadership drove early NSDAP growth vs View 2 argues nationalist anger in the 25-Point Programme and SA brawling mattered more.

children.label: Hitler, DAP & Setting Up NSDAP
children.gloss: Hitler's early career moved from joining Anton Drexler's German Workers' Party in 1919 to setting up and leading the Nazi Party.

children.label: Army Spy Joined Drexler's Tiny DAP
children.gloss: Monitored Munich radicals (Sept 1919); Shared fierce anti-Versailles anger.

children.label: Swastika Branding & 1921 Takeover
children.gloss: Designed red-white-black swastika flag; Bought Völkischer Beobachter newspaper.

children.label: Oratory & Führerprinzip Built Unity
children.gloss: Ousted Drexler as sole leader (1921); Beer-hall speeches drew 55,000 by 1923.

children.label: Bavarian Right-Wing Climate Fed DAP
children.gloss: Post-Soviet turmoil radicalised Munich; Sympathetic elites sheltered nationalists.

children.label: 25-Point Programme & the SA
children.gloss: In 1920–21 the Twenty-Five Point Programme defined Nazi ideology while Ernst Röhm's SA policed streets and rallies.

children.label: Blended Nationalism & Worker Pledges
children.gloss: Scrap Versailles & strip Jewish rights; Promised profit-sharing & old-age aid.

children.label: Röhm Formed Brownshirt Stormtroopers
children.gloss: Recruited jobless ex-Freikorps (Aug 1921); Guarded rallies & beat KPD rivals.

children.label: Broad Manifesto Caught Angry Voters
children.gloss: Attacked big stores & Versailles terms; Appealed to clerks, artisans & workers.

children.label: Rowdy SA Thugs Alienated Moderates
children.gloss: Street violence scared middle classes; Kept NSDAP a Bavarian regional fringe.

children.label: Kept NSDAP a Bavarian regional fringe
children.gloss: Kept NSDAP a Bavarian regional fringe

children.label: 2.2 Munich Putsch & Lean Years
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues the 1923 Munich Putsch was a disastrous armed failure followed by 2.6% irrelevance vs View 2 argues trial fame, Mein Kampf, and Bamberg reorganisation forged future victory.

children.label: Munich Putsch Causes & Defeat
children.gloss: Hyperinflation, Stresemann ending Ruhr resistance, and Mussolini's Rome march triggered the failed 1923 Munich Putsch.

children.label: Ruhr Surrender & Impatient 50,000 SA
children.gloss: Anger over ending Ruhr strike (1923); Inspired by Mussolini; feared SA split.

children.label: Inspired by Mussolini; feared SA split
children.gloss: Inspired by Mussolini; feared SA split

children.label: Sixteen Nazis Shot in Munich Streets
children.gloss: Kahr & Lossow alerted Bavarian police; 2,000 marchers scattered; NSDAP banned.

children.label: Amateur Planning Wrecked the Coup
children.gloss: Left army barracks & telegraphs free; Hitler fled with dislocated shoulder.

children.label: → Shifted NSDAP to Legal Reorganisation
children.gloss: Proved armed coups failed sans army; Pivoted Hitler to winning Reichstag votes.

children.label: Proved armed coups failed sans army
children.gloss: Proved armed coups failed sans army

children.label: Pivoted Hitler to winning Reichstag votes
children.gloss: Pivoted Hitler to winning Reichstag votes

children.label: Treason Trial & Mein Kampf
children.gloss: Long-term consequences of the Munich Putsch included nationwide trial publicity, lenient imprisonment, and Mein Kampf.

children.label: Right-Wing Judges Sympathised Openly
children.gloss: 24-day trial became media platform; Served 9 months in Landsberg prison.

children.label: Dictated Mein Kampf to Rudolf Hess
children.gloss: Aryan race dogma & eastern Lebensraum; Rejected democracy for Führer rule.

children.label: Turned Hitler into a National Star
children.gloss: Front-page press coverage nationwide; Crowned leader of extreme German right.

children.label: Crowned leader of extreme German right
children.gloss: Crowned leader of extreme German right

children.label: Party Split While Hitler Was Jailed
children.gloss: Northern & southern factions quarrelled; Banned movement lost voters in 1924.

children.label: Lean Years & Bamberg Conference
children.gloss: Limited support for the Nazi Party in 1924–28 accompanied nationwide Party reorganisation and the Bamberg Conference of 1926.

children.label: Weimar Prosperity Starved Extremism
children.gloss: Stable Rentenmark & rising real wages; Locarno peace calmed nationalist anger.

children.label: 1926 Bamberg Beat Gregor Strasser
children.gloss: Crushed socialist land-reform wing; Built 35 Gaue; won over Goebbels.

children.label: Crushed to 12 Seats in May 1928
children.gloss: Won just 2.6% despite 100k members; Propaganda failed during Golden Years.

children.label: → National Machine Ready for 1929 Slump
children.gloss: Gauleiters & Hitler Youth spanned Reich; Rural network primed for 1929 crash.

children.label: 2.3 Depression & Nazi Surge
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues Great Depression unemployment and fear of Communism drove voters to the Nazis vs View 2 argues Hitler's charisma, Goebbels' modern propaganda, and SA order won support.

children.label: Mass Unemployment & KPD Growth
children.gloss: The Wall Street Crash caused soaring unemployment and growing support for the Communist Party across industrial cities.

children.label: US Banks Recalled Short-Term Loans
children.gloss: Oct 1929 Crash drained factory credit; Industrial output halved by winter 1932.

children.label: → Unemployment Fuelled 1930–32 Nazi Vote
children.gloss: Brüning's 66 decrees slashed welfare; 6 million jobless turned to radicals.

children.label: 100 KPD Seats Scared Middle Classes
children.gloss: Jobless city workers backed Communists; Panicked farmers, clerks & industrialists.

children.label: Slump Alone Did Not Pick the Winner
children.gloss: Depression discredited Weimar moderates; Goebbels out-organised rival rightists.

children.label: Hitler's Appeal & Propaganda
children.gloss: Growth in support for the Nazi Party stemmed from the personal appeal of Hitler and the Nazis and Goebbels' propaganda.

children.label: Tailored Promises to Every Class
children.gloss: 'Work and Bread' for the unemployed; Farm debt relief & anti-union order.

children.label: Hitler Over Germany Flight Campaign
children.gloss: Flew across 20 cities in days; Radio broadcasts & torchlit parades.

children.label: Votes Only Exploded After 1929 Crash
children.gloss: Leapt 12 to 230 seats (1928–32); Mirrored rising joblessness line-for-line.

children.label: Strongman Image Inspired Mass Hope
children.gloss: 13.4m voted Hitler for President (1932); Dynamic rallies shamed weak coalitions.

children.label: Work of the SA & Street Order
children.gloss: The disciplined work of the SA reinforced Nazi growth by intimidating Communist rivals and running soup kitchens.

children.label: 400,000 SA Paraded Visible Strength
children.gloss: Soup kitchens fed jobless young men; Uniformed marches projected discipline.

children.label: Soup kitchens fed jobless young men
children.gloss: Soup kitchens fed jobless young men

children.label: Smashed KPD Red Front Meetings
children.gloss: Deadly Prussian street battles (1932); Convinced elites only Nazis beat Reds.

children.label: Convinced elites only Nazis beat Reds
children.gloss: Convinced elites only Nazis beat Reds

children.label: Fear of Communism Drove SA Support
children.gloss: Voters excused Brownshirt street violence; Dreaded Bolshevik-style Red revolution.

children.label: Paramilitary Muscle Crushed Rivals
children.gloss: Ripped down SPD and KPD posters; Intimidated democratic town rallies.

children.label: Ripped down SPD and KPD posters
children.gloss: Ripped down SPD and KPD posters

children.label: 2.4 Hitler Becomes Chancellor
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues backstairs intrigue by von Papen and Hindenburg handed power to a fading movement vs View 2 argues leading the largest Reichstag party made Hitler impossible to ignore.

children.label: 1932 Presidential & Reichstag Vote
children.gloss: The Presidential and Reichstag elections of 1932 made the Nazis Germany's largest party before dipping in November.

children.label: 230 Seats → Deadlocked Weimar Rule
children.gloss: 37.3% peak made NSDAP largest party; Speaker Göring blocked rival cabinets.

children.label: Dropped to 196 Seats in November
children.gloss: Shed 2m votes in November 1932; Drained party funds; Strasser split.

children.label: Nazi Vote Had Already Peaked
children.gloss: Campaign fatigue & SA violence hurt; Needed elite rescue by late 1932.

children.label: Still Far Ahead of Every Rival
children.gloss: 196 seats outstripped SPD and KPD; Starved Papen & Schleicher of majorities.

children.label: Hindenburg, Papen & Jan 1933
children.gloss: Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 through the roles of Hindenburg, Kurt von Schleicher, and Franz von Papen.

children.label: Schleicher Failed to Split the Nazis
children.gloss: Hitler blocked Strasser deal (Dec 1932); Schleicher lost Hindenburg's confidence.

children.label: Secret Pact at Schröder's Villa
children.gloss: Papen agreed coalition (Jan 1933); Only 2 other Nazis in Cabinet.

children.label: Papen Boasted of Taming Hitler
children.gloss: Vowed to 'push Hitler into corner'; Fatal conservative elite miscalculation.

children.label: → Appointed Chancellor (30 Jan 1933)
children.gloss: Hindenburg swore Hitler in legally; Only leader commanding mass millions.

children.label: KT3: Nazi Dictatorship
children.gloss: Key topic 3: Nazi control and dictatorship, 1933–39 — dismantling democracy in 1933–34, the SS-Gestapo police state, Goebbels' propaganda and Church controls, and pre-war opposition.

children.label: 3.1 Creating a Dictatorship
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues pseudo-legal decrees and the Enabling Act built Hitler's dictatorship vs View 2 argues ruthless SA violence and the Night of the Long Knives sealed absolute power.

children.label: Reichstag Fire & Emergency Decree
children.gloss: The Reichstag Fire of 27 February 1933 let Hitler suspend civil liberties and crush Communists before March elections.

children.label: Van der Lubbe Arrested in Flames
children.gloss: Dutch communist caught (27 Feb 1933); Göring claimed Red uprising had begun.

children.label: Göring claimed Red uprising had begun
children.gloss: Göring claimed Red uprising had begun

children.label: 4,000 KPD Leaders Jailed Overnight
children.gloss: 28 Feb Fire Decree suspended rights; Abolished free press & trial rights.

children.label: → Paved Way for March 1933 Enabling Act
children.gloss: Secured 43.9% in March 1933 vote; Detained KPD deputies before key vote.

children.label: Detained KPD deputies before key vote
children.gloss: Detained KPD deputies before key vote

children.label: 50,000 SA Auxiliaries Used Terror
children.gloss: Göring armed Prussian SA as police; 70 opponents killed during campaign.

children.label: Göring armed Prussian SA as police
children.gloss: Göring armed Prussian SA as police

children.label: Enabling Act, Parties & Unions
children.gloss: The Enabling Act led rapidly to the banning of other parties and trade unions during Gleichschaltung in 1933.

children.label: 444–94 Vote Ended Reichstag Rule
children.gloss: 81 KPD barred; Centre Party swayed; 4-year Cabinet decree rule (23 Mar).

children.label: → Crushed Unions & Outlawed All Rivals
children.gloss: Trade unions crushed on 2 May; Länder dissolved; parties banned (July).

children.label: Constitutional Two-Thirds Law
children.gloss: Enacted laws without Reichstag votes; Bypassed Hindenburg's presidential check.

children.label: Armed SA Chanted Inside Kroll Opera
children.gloss: Only 94 SPD deputies voted against; Stormtroopers threatened MPs inside hall.

children.label: Long Knives, Führer & Army Oath
children.gloss: Crushing the threat from Röhm and the SA in the Night of the Long Knives preceded Hindenburg's death, Hitler becoming Führer, and the army oath of allegiance.

children.label: Röhm's 3m SA Threatened the Army
children.gloss: Röhm demanded 'Second Revolution' merge; 100,000-man Reichswehr feared SA takeover.

children.label: Röhm Purge → Führer & Army Oath
children.gloss: SS executed Röhm & ~400 rivals; Hindenburg died; army swore Hitler oath.

children.label: Hindenburg died; army swore Hitler oath
children.gloss: Hindenburg died; army swore Hitler oath

children.label: Plebiscite & Oath Legalised Führer
children.gloss: 90% backed Führer role (Aug 1934); Bound troops personally to Adolf Hitler.

children.label: Bound troops personally to Adolf Hitler
children.gloss: Bound troops personally to Adolf Hitler

children.label: Cold-Blooded Murder Above the Law
children.gloss: Opponents executed without any trial; Proved SS violence underpinned rule.

children.label: 3.2 The Nazi Police State
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues omnipotent SS, Gestapo, camp, and court terror crushed freedom from above vs View 2 argues a small Gestapo relied heavily on voluntary civilian denunciations from below.

children.label: Gestapo, SS & Concentration Camps
children.gloss: Heinrich Himmler's SS, Reinhard Heydrich's Gestapo, and concentration camps enforced the Nazi police state.

children.label: Protective Custody Without Trial
children.gloss: Tapped phones & intercepted private mail; Sent suspects straight to Dachau camp.

children.label: Sent suspects straight to Dachau camp
children.gloss: Sent suspects straight to Dachau camp

children.label: 240,000 SS & Six Major Camps by 1939
children.gloss: Himmler's Death's Head camp guards; Held Reds, socialists & 'asocials'.

children.label: Midnight Arrests Silenced Critics
children.gloss: Rumours of camp torture spread terror; Kept political doubts behind closed doors.

children.label: Rumours of camp torture spread terror
children.gloss: Rumours of camp torture spread terror

children.label: Kept political doubts behind closed doors
children.gloss: Kept political doubts behind closed doors

children.label: 32,000 Gestapo Policed 70m Citizens
children.gloss: Over half of tips from neighbours; Block wardens monitored local flats.

children.label: Over half of tips from neighbours
children.gloss: Over half of tips from neighbours

children.label: Nazi Control of the Legal System
children.gloss: Nazi control of the legal system abolished judicial independence and turned courts into instruments of political terror.

children.label: Judges Forced into Nazi Law League
children.gloss: Sacked Jewish & democratic magistrates; Punished any act against Hitler's will.

children.label: Punished any act against Hitler's will
children.gloss: Punished any act against Hitler's will

children.label: People's Court & 46 Capital Crimes
children.gloss: 1934 treason court had zero juries; Executions soared from 8 to hundreds.

children.label: Destroyed Rule of Law Completely
children.gloss: Jailed for anti-Hitler jokes or radio; No right to appeal Special Courts.

children.label: Jailed for anti-Hitler jokes or radio

children.label: No right to appeal Special Courts
children.gloss: No right to appeal Special Courts

children.label: Conservatives Backed Tough Courts
children.gloss: Harsh penalties on Communists & crime; Matched conservative desire for order.

children.label: 3.3 Propaganda, Culture & Church
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues Goebbels' propaganda, censorship, rallies, and Church policies reshaped German minds vs View 2 argues propaganda reinforced old nationalism while failing to crush Christian faith.

children.label: Goebbels, Censorship & Nazi Media
children.gloss: Goebbels and the Ministry of Propaganda enforced strict censorship alongside Nazi use of radio and newspaper media.

children.label: Editors' Law Silenced Free Press
children.gloss: Closed 1,600 opposition newspapers; Daily Ministry orders set headlines.

children.label: 70% Owned Cheap People's Receivers
children.gloss: Volksempfänger blocked foreign stations; 6,000 street speakers aired speeches.

children.label: Built Unrivalled Führer Myth Cult
children.gloss: Shielded Hitler from everyday blame; Rallied mass backing for foreign aims.

children.label: Rallied mass backing for foreign aims
children.gloss: Rallied mass backing for foreign aims

children.label: Boring Uniform Press Lost Readers
children.gloss: Newspaper circulation dropped by 10%; Listeners preferred music over lectures.

children.label: Nuremberg Rallies & 1936 Olympics
children.gloss: Spectacular Nuremberg rallies and international sport at the 1936 Berlin Olympics showcased Nazi strength and unity.

children.label: Speer's Cathedral of Light Spectacle
children.gloss: Searchlights & 100,000 Nuremberg marchers; Fostered emotional national belonging.

children.label: Berlin Stadium Topped 1936 Medals
children.gloss: Anti-Jewish signs hidden (Aug 1936); Germany won 33 Olympic gold medals.

children.label: Dazzled Guests & Boosted Pride
children.gloss: Riefenstahl films & TV cameras dazzled; Impressed foreign press & tourists.

children.label: Jesse Owens Mocked Aryan Supremacy
children.gloss: Black US sprinter won 4 golds; Visibly refuted Nazi racial dogma.

children.label: Control of Culture, Art & Film
children.gloss: Nazi control of culture and the arts policed art, monumental architecture, literature, and cinema through the Reich Chamber.

children.label: Reich Chamber Licensed Every Creator
children.gloss: Expelled 2,500 writers; banned jazz; Enforced 'Blood and Soil' themes.

children.label: Book Burnings & 1,300 Vetted Films
children.gloss: Students burned 20,000 books (May 1933); Speer halls & Goebbels script checks.

children.label: Cinema Escapism & Rally Films Worked
children.gloss: Subtle nationalism in light comedies; 400m German cinema visits by 1938.

children.label: 2m Queued for Degenerate Art Show
children.gloss: 1937 Munich banned-art show packed; Drew 3x official Nazi art gallery.

children.label: The Concordat & the Reich Church
children.gloss: Nazi attempts to control the Catholic and Protestant Churches used the 1933 Concordat and Ludwig Müller's Reich Church.

children.label: 45m Protestants & 22m Catholics
children.gloss: Christian ethics rivalled Nazi loyalty; Hitler moved to neutralise churches.

children.label: → Broken Pacts Sparked Church Defiance
children.gloss: Nazis shut Catholic schools & youth; Reich Bishop Müller banned Old Testament.

children.label: Reich Bishop Müller banned Old Testament
children.gloss: Reich Bishop Müller banned Old Testament

children.label: Concordat Ended Catholic Politics
children.gloss: July 1933 Vatican pact ended Centre; 2,000 pastors joined German Christians.

children.label: Only 5% Joined Nazi Pagan Faith
children.gloss: Over 90% stayed church members (1939); Thousands rejected Reich Bishop Müller.

children.label: 3.4 Opposition & Conformity
children.gloss: Q3d Core Debate: View 1 argues genuine gratitude for jobs and national pride kept pre-war opposition tiny vs View 2 argues Gestapo terror forced outward conformity despite brave Church and youth defiance.

children.label: Conformity & Scale of Support
children.gloss: The high scale of support for the Nazi regime combined popular national pride with fear, limiting underground opposition.

children.label: Full Employment & Foreign Triumphs
children.gloss: Jobs & 1936 Rhineland won pride; Genuine admiration from millions.

children.label: Exiled SPD Sopade Smuggled Leaflets
children.gloss: Socialist & KPD couriers hid pamphlets; Gestapo raids smashed underground cells.

children.label: Führer Popularity & Votes Held Firm
